notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Force is a push or pull acting on a body.
  • Force can change the state of rest of a body.
  • Force can change the speed of a moving body.
  • Force can change the direction of motion.
  • Force can change the shape or size of a body.
  • Force is a vector quantity.
  • Force has both magnitude and direction.
  • The SI unit of force is newton.
  • Force is commonly represented by F.
  • One newton is the force required to produce an acceleration of 1 m/s² in a mass of 1 kg.
  • 1 N = 1 kg m/s².
  • A force produces acceleration only when there is a non-zero resultant force.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Force → Push/Pull → Change in Motion or Shape

2. Effects of Force
  • Force can start a stationary object moving.
  • Force can stop a moving object.
  • Force can increase speed.
  • Force can decrease speed.
  • Force can change direction.
  • Force can deform an object.
  • A force does not always produce visible motion.
  • A force may be balanced by another force.
  • Balanced forces can deform an object even when they produce no acceleration.
3. Resultant Force
  • Resultant force is the single force equivalent to the combined effect of all forces acting on a body.
  • Resultant force is also called net force.
  • Forces acting in the same direction are added.
  • Oppositely directed forces are subtracted.
  • If resultant force is zero, acceleration is zero.
  • If resultant force is non-zero, the body accelerates.
  • Acceleration occurs in the direction of the resultant force.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Net Force = 0 → No acceleration

Net Force ≠ 0 → Acceleration

4. Balanced Forces
  • Balanced forces have zero resultant.
  • Balanced forces do not change the velocity of a body.
  • A stationary body remains stationary under balanced forces.
  • A moving body continues with constant velocity under balanced forces.
  • Balanced forces may still change shape.
  • A book resting on a table is an example of balanced forces.
  • The downward weight of the book is balanced by the upward normal reaction.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Balanced force does not necessarily mean that no forces are acting.

5. Unbalanced Forces
  • Unbalanced forces produce a non-zero resultant force.
  • An unbalanced force produces acceleration.
  • Acceleration may involve an increase in speed.
  • Acceleration may involve a decrease in speed.
  • Acceleration may involve a change in direction.
  • A moving vehicle accelerating forward experiences an unbalanced resultant force.
6. Contact Forces
  • Contact forces require physical interaction between bodies.
  • Friction is a contact force.
  • Normal reaction is a contact force.
  • Tension is a contact force.
  • Spring force is a contact force.
  • Applied force is generally a contact force.
  • Air resistance is a contact force.
  • Buoyant force arises from contact with a fluid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Contact Force → Physical contact required

7. Non-Contact Forces
  • Non-contact forces can act without direct physical contact.
  • Gravitational force is a non-contact force.
  • Electrostatic force is a non-contact force.
  • Magnetic force can act without physical contact.
  • These interactions can be described using fields.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Non-Contact → Gravity + Electric + Magnetic

8. Fundamental Forces of Nature
  • Four fundamental interactions are recognised in modern physics.
  • They are gravitational force, electromagnetic force, strong nuclear force and weak nuclear force.
  • All ordinary contact forces arise ultimately from electromagnetic interactions between atoms and molecules.
  • The strong and weak interactions act mainly at subatomic scales.
  • Gravity acts between objects possessing mass-energy.
  • Electromagnetism acts between electrically charged particles.
📌 Must-Memorise

1. Gravitational force

2. Electromagnetic force

3. Strong nuclear force

4. Weak nuclear force

9. Gravitational Force
  • Gravitational force is an attractive force.
  • Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass.
  • Newton formulated the universal law of gravitation.
  • Gravity keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
  • Gravity keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth.
  • Gravity gives objects weight.
  • Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental interactions at the particle scale.
  • Gravity has an effectively infinite range.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gravity → Mass → Always Attractive

10. Electromagnetic Force
  • Electromagnetic force acts between electrically charged particles.
  • Electric and magnetic phenomena are manifestations of the electromagnetic interaction.
  • Like electric charges repel.
  • Unlike electric charges attract.
  • Electromagnetic interaction has an effectively infinite range.
  • Friction, tension and normal force arise ultimately from electromagnetic interactions at the atomic level.
  • Electromagnetic force is much stronger than gravity at atomic scales.
11. Strong Nuclear Force
  • Strong nuclear interaction is the strongest fundamental interaction.
  • It acts over a very short range.
  • At the quark level, the strong interaction binds quarks inside protons and neutrons.
  • The residual strong nuclear force helps bind protons and neutrons within atomic nuclei.
  • It overcomes electrostatic repulsion among protons at nuclear distances.
  • Its effective nuclear range is of the order of 10⁻¹⁵ m.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Strong Force → Strongest → Holds nucleus together

12. Weak Nuclear Force
  • Weak nuclear interaction acts at extremely short distances.
  • It is involved in beta radioactive decay.
  • It plays an important role in nuclear reactions in stars.
  • Weak interactions can change one type of elementary particle into another.
  • The weak interaction is stronger than gravity but weaker than strong and electromagnetic interactions at typical particle scales.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Weak Force → Beta Decay

13. Relative Strength — Basic Order
  • Strong nuclear interaction is the strongest fundamental interaction.
  • Electromagnetic interaction is weaker than the strong interaction.
  • Weak interaction is much weaker than electromagnetic interaction.
  • Gravity is the weakest at subatomic scales.
📌 Remember

Strong → Electromagnetic → Weak → Gravity

14. Newton's First Law
  • Newton's First Law is called the Law of Inertia.
  • A body at rest remains at rest unless acted upon by a net external force.
  • A body in uniform straight-line motion continues in that state unless acted upon by a net external force.
  • The First Law defines inertial motion.
  • The First Law explains why force is required to change velocity rather than merely maintain motion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton I → Inertia

15. Inertia
  • Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of motion.
  • Mass is a measure of inertia.
  • Greater mass means greater inertia.
  • A stationary object resists being set into motion.
  • A moving object resists changes in speed or direction.
  • Inertia itself is not a force.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Inertia → Property of matter.

Inertia ≠ Force.

16. Inertia of Rest
  • Inertia of rest is the tendency of a stationary body to remain stationary.
  • A passenger may fall backward when a stationary bus starts suddenly.
  • Dust separates from a carpet when the carpet is beaten.
  • Fruits may fall when a tree branch is shaken suddenly.
17. Inertia of Motion
  • Inertia of motion is the tendency of a moving body to continue moving with the same velocity.
  • Passengers tend to fall forward when a moving bus stops suddenly.
  • Luggage may move forward when a vehicle brakes suddenly.
  • Seat belts protect passengers by restraining their continued forward motion.
18. Inertia of Direction
  • Inertia of direction is resistance to a change in direction of motion.
  • Mud flies tangentially from a rotating tyre.
  • A passenger may feel thrown sideways when a vehicle turns sharply.
  • Objects released from circular motion move approximately tangentially.
19. Newton's Second Law
  • Newton's Second Law relates force to change in momentum.
  • The net force acting on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum.
  • For constant mass, F = ma.
  • F is force.
  • m is mass.
  • a is acceleration.
  • Acceleration is directly proportional to net force for fixed mass.
  • Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass for a fixed force.
  • Acceleration occurs in the direction of the net force.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton II → F = ma

20. Definition of One Newton
  • One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
  • 1 N = 1 kg m/s².
  • Newton is a derived SI unit.
  • The unit is named after Isaac Newton.
21. Newton's Third Law
  • For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
  • Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude.
  • They act in opposite directions.
  • They act simultaneously.
  • They act on different bodies.
  • Action and reaction are forces of the same interaction.
  • Action-reaction forces do not cancel because they act on different objects.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Action and reaction → Different bodies.

22. Newton's Third Law — Applications
  • Walking depends on Newton's Third Law.
  • A person pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes the person forward.
  • Swimming depends on action and reaction.
  • A swimmer pushes water backward and water pushes the swimmer forward.
  • Birds push air downward and backward while flying.
  • Rocket propulsion demonstrates action and reaction.
  • Gun recoil demonstrates action and reaction.
23. Momentum
  • Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
  • Momentum is represented by p.
  • p = mv.
  • Momentum is a vector quantity.
  • SI unit is kg m/s.
  • A stationary body has zero momentum.
  • Greater mass produces greater momentum at the same velocity.
  • Greater velocity produces greater momentum for the same mass.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Momentum → p = mv

24. Conservation of Momentum
  • Total linear momentum remains constant in an isolated system.
  • Conservation of momentum applies when net external force is zero.
  • Momentum before an isolated collision equals momentum after the collision.
  • Gun recoil illustrates conservation of momentum.
  • Rocket motion illustrates conservation of momentum.
  • Momentum is conserved in both elastic and inelastic isolated collisions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Momentum → Conserved in isolated elastic and inelastic collisions.

25. Impulse
  • Impulse is force multiplied by the time interval for which it acts.
  • For constant force, J = FΔt.
  • Impulse equals change in momentum.
  • J = Δp.
  • SI unit is newton-second.
  • 1 N s is equivalent to 1 kg m/s.
  • A large force acting for a short time can produce the same impulse as a smaller force acting for a longer time.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Impulse → Force × Time → Change in Momentum

26. Impulse Applications
  • Airbags increase the time over which a passenger's momentum changes.
  • Increasing stopping time reduces average impact force.
  • Seat belts reduce injury by increasing stopping time and distributing force.
  • A cricketer moves the hands backward while catching a ball.
  • A high jumper lands on a soft mat to increase stopping time.
  • Packaging materials protect fragile objects by extending impact time.
📌 Remember

Same Δp + Longer time → Smaller average force

27. Applied Force
  • Applied force is an external push or pull exerted directly on an object.
  • Pushing a trolley applies force to it.
  • Pulling a suitcase applies force.
  • Applied force may be balanced or unbalanced depending on other forces.
28. Normal Force
  • Normal force is exerted by a surface on an object in contact with it.
  • It acts perpendicular to the surface.
  • A table exerts an upward normal force on a book resting on it.
  • Normal force is not always equal to weight.
  • On an inclined plane, normal reaction is generally less than mg when no additional forces act perpendicular to the surface.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Normal force ≠ Always weight.

29. Tension
  • Tension is a pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, cable or similar object.
  • Tension acts along the length of the string.
  • An ideal massless string is often assumed to have uniform tension.
  • Strings can transmit pulling force but ordinarily cannot push.
30. Spring Force
  • A stretched or compressed spring exerts a restoring force.
  • Within the elastic range, spring force follows Hooke's Law.
  • F = −kx is the vector form for ideal spring restoring force.
  • k is the spring constant.
  • x is displacement from equilibrium.
  • The negative sign indicates force opposite to displacement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spring Force → Hooke's Law → Restoring Force

31. Friction
  • Friction opposes relative motion or tendency of relative motion between contacting surfaces.
  • Friction is a contact force.
  • Friction acts parallel to the contact surface.
  • Friction may produce heat.
  • Friction is essential for walking.
  • Friction allows tyres to grip roads.
  • Friction enables brakes to stop vehicles.
  • Excessive friction causes wear and energy loss.
32. Static Friction
  • Static friction acts when surfaces are not sliding relative to each other.
  • Static friction adjusts in magnitude up to a maximum value.
  • It opposes the tendency to slide.
  • Walking normally depends mainly on static friction between foot and ground.
33. Limiting Friction
  • Limiting friction is the maximum static friction just before sliding begins.
  • In the simple dry-friction model, limiting friction is proportional to normal reaction.
  • Flim = μsN.
  • μs is the coefficient of static friction.
  • The coefficient of friction has no unit.
34. Kinetic Friction
  • Kinetic or sliding friction acts when two surfaces slide relative to each other.
  • Kinetic friction is generally lower than maximum static friction for the same surfaces.
  • Sliding a box along a floor involves kinetic friction.
35. Rolling Friction
  • Rolling friction opposes rolling motion.
  • Rolling friction is generally smaller than sliding friction.
  • Wheels reduce resistance by replacing sliding with rolling.
  • Ball bearings reduce friction by using rolling elements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rolling Friction < Sliding Friction generally

36. Factors Affecting Friction
  • Friction depends on the nature of contacting surfaces.
  • Roughness and material properties affect friction.
  • In simple models, friction increases with normal force.
  • Friction is approximately independent of apparent contact area for ideal dry rigid surfaces, though real materials can behave more complexly.
  • Lubricants reduce friction.
37. Advantages of Friction
  • Walking requires friction.
  • Writing requires friction between pen or pencil and paper.
  • Vehicles accelerate because tyres grip the road.
  • Brakes work through friction.
  • Nails and screws are held partly because of friction.
  • Matches ignite because friction generates heat.
38. Disadvantages of Friction
  • Friction causes wear of moving parts.
  • Friction produces unwanted heat.
  • Friction reduces machine efficiency.
  • Friction increases fuel and energy consumption.
  • Lubrication reduces unwanted friction.
39. Reducing Friction
  • Lubricants reduce direct contact between surfaces.
  • Ball bearings reduce sliding friction.
  • Streamlining reduces fluid drag.
  • Polishing can reduce roughness.
  • Air cushions can reduce surface contact.
  • Low-friction materials are used in machines.
40. Increasing Friction
  • Tyres have treads to improve grip.
  • Shoe soles are textured to increase friction.
  • Spikes increase friction with the ground.
  • Sand is spread on slippery surfaces.
  • Brake pads use high-friction materials.
41. Drag Force
  • Drag is the resistance exerted by a fluid on a body moving through it.
  • Air resistance is a type of drag.
  • Water resistance is a type of drag.
  • Drag generally increases with speed.
  • Streamlining reduces drag.
  • Drag acts opposite the relative motion through the fluid.
42. Terminal Velocity
  • A falling object in a fluid may reach terminal velocity.
  • At terminal velocity, downward weight is balanced by upward drag and buoyancy.
  • Net force becomes zero.
  • Acceleration becomes zero.
  • Speed remains constant.
  • Parachutes reduce terminal velocity by increasing drag.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Terminal Velocity → Forces Balanced → a = 0

43. Gravitational Force
  • Gravitational force acts between all objects with mass.
  • It is always attractive in Newtonian gravity.
  • Gravitational force decreases as distance increases.
  • Newton's universal gravitation law applies to point masses and spherically symmetric bodies under appropriate conditions.
  • Gravity controls much of the large-scale structure and orbital motion in astronomy.
44. Universal Law of Gravitation
  • F = Gm₁m₂/r².
  • F is gravitational force.
  • G is universal gravitational constant.
  • m₁ and m₂ are the interacting masses.
  • r is distance between their centres.
  • Force is directly proportional to the product of masses.
  • Force is inversely proportional to the square of distance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Distance × 2 → Gravitational force becomes 1/4

45. Universal Gravitational Constant
  • G is the universal gravitational constant.
  • Its value is approximately 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
  • G is the same constant in Newton's law of universal gravitation.
  • Henry Cavendish's torsion-balance experiment enabled the gravitational interaction between laboratory masses to be measured accurately.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

G ≈ 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg²

46. Acceleration Due to Gravity
  • Acceleration produced by Earth's gravitational field is represented by g.
  • Near Earth's surface, g is approximately 9.8 m/s².
  • g varies slightly with location.
  • g decreases with altitude.
  • g decreases toward zero as one moves toward Earth's centre.
  • g is greater near the poles than near the equator.
  • Earth's rotation contributes to the lower effective g near the equator.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth g → ~9.8 m/s²

47. G vs g
  • G is the universal gravitational constant.
  • g is acceleration due to gravity at a particular location.
  • G has a fixed universal value in classical gravitation.
  • g varies with planet, altitude, latitude and depth.
  • SI unit of G is N m² kg⁻².
  • SI unit of g is m/s².
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

G ≠ g

48. Mass vs Weight
  • Mass is a measure of inertia.
  • SI unit of mass is kilogram.
  • Mass is a scalar quantity.
  • Weight is gravitational force.
  • Weight = mg.
  • SI unit of weight is newton.
  • Weight is a vector.
  • Mass remains nearly constant with location in ordinary mechanics.
  • Weight changes when g changes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mass → kg

Weight → N

49. Weight on the Moon
  • Lunar gravity is approximately one-sixth of Earth's surface gravity.
  • A person's mass remains the same on Earth and Moon.
  • The person's weight on the Moon is approximately one-sixth of Earth weight.
  • Jumping is easier on the Moon because gravitational acceleration is lower.
50. Free Fall
  • Free fall is motion under gravity alone.
  • In vacuum, all bodies at the same location fall with the same gravitational acceleration regardless of mass.
  • Galileo's studies challenged the belief that heavier bodies necessarily fall faster.
  • Differences in ordinary falling speeds often result from air resistance.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

In vacuum → Heavy and light objects fall with same g.

51. Centripetal Force
  • Centripetal force is the net inward force required for circular motion.
  • It acts toward the centre of the circular path.
  • F = mv²/r.
  • Centripetal force is not a separate fundamental force.
  • Gravity can act as centripetal force.
  • Friction can act as centripetal force.
  • Tension can act as centripetal force.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Centripetal → Centre-seeking

52. Centrifugal Force
  • Centrifugal force is an apparent outward force introduced in a rotating reference frame.
  • It is a pseudo force.
  • It is opposite in direction to centripetal acceleration.
  • The outward feeling experienced in a turning vehicle is associated with inertia and the rotating frame.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Centripetal → Inward resultant force.

Centrifugal → Apparent outward pseudo force.

53. Circular Motion and Friction
  • A vehicle turning on a level road requires an inward force.
  • Static friction between tyres and road can provide this centripetal force.
  • Insufficient friction can cause skidding.
  • Wet or icy roads reduce available friction.
  • Banking helps provide inward force with less dependence on friction.
54. Banking of Roads
  • Roads are banked at curves to improve safety.
  • The outer edge is raised relative to the inner edge.
  • A component of normal reaction acts toward the centre of the curve.
  • Banking reduces dependence on tyre-road friction.
  • Higher-speed curves generally require greater banking for a specified radius.
55. Magnetic Force
  • Magnetic force acts on moving electric charges and magnetic materials.
  • A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field.
  • A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field can experience force.
  • Electric motors operate using magnetic force on current-carrying conductors.
  • Magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to velocity when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the motion.
56. Force on Current-Carrying Conductor
  • A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences force when appropriately oriented.
  • The direction of force can be determined using Fleming's Left-Hand Rule in motor applications.
  • The magnitude depends on current, field strength, conductor length and orientation.
  • Electric motors convert electrical energy into mechanical energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fleming Left Hand → Motor

57. Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
  • Fleming's Left-Hand Rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
  • Forefinger represents magnetic field.
  • Middle finger represents current.
  • Thumb represents force or motion.
  • The three directions are mutually perpendicular.
📌 Remember

Left Hand → Motor

58. Electrostatic Force
  • Electrostatic force acts between electric charges.
  • Like charges repel.
  • Unlike charges attract.
  • Coulomb's Law describes force between point charges.
  • Electrostatic force follows an inverse-square relationship.
59. Coulomb's Law
  • Electrostatic force is directly proportional to the product of the charges.
  • It is inversely proportional to the square of distance.
  • F = kq₁q₂/r² in magnitude.
  • Charles-Augustin de Coulomb is associated with the law.
  • The SI unit of electric charge is coulomb.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coulomb → Electric Force → Inverse Square

60. Gravitational vs Electrostatic Force
  • Both can act over very large distances.
  • Both obey inverse-square laws in their classical forms.
  • Gravity acts on mass-energy and is attractive between ordinary positive masses.
  • Electrostatic force acts on electric charges.
  • Electrostatic force may be attractive or repulsive.
  • Electrostatic interaction is enormously stronger than gravity between elementary charged particles.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Gravity → Attractive.

Electric force → Attractive or repulsive.

61. Buoyant Force
  • Buoyant force is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed object.
  • It arises because fluid pressure increases with depth.
  • Archimedes' Principle gives its magnitude.
  • Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid.
  • Buoyancy acts in both liquids and gases.
62. Lift Force
  • Lift is a force acting approximately perpendicular to the relative flow of a fluid around a body.
  • Aircraft wings generate lift by redirecting airflow and creating pressure differences.
  • Bernoulli-related pressure effects form part of the explanation of aerodynamic lift.
  • Angle of attack influences lift.
  • Excessive angle of attack can cause aerodynamic stall.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Aircraft lift cannot be explained solely by saying “air above the wing travels farther and therefore must travel faster.”

63. Thrust
  • Thrust is a force that propels an object.
  • Propellers generate thrust by accelerating fluid backward.
  • Jet engines generate thrust by expelling gases backward.
  • Rockets generate thrust by expelling exhaust gases.
  • Rocket thrust works even in vacuum.
  • Rockets do not need air to push against.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rocket → Expel gases → Reaction thrust

64. Rocket Propulsion
  • Rocket propulsion follows conservation of momentum.
  • It also illustrates Newton's Third Law.
  • Hot gases are expelled backward at high speed.
  • The rocket gains forward momentum.
  • Rockets can operate in space because thrust results from momentum exchange with exhaust.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rocket does not require atmospheric air for reaction force.

65. Recoil of Gun
  • When a bullet moves forward, the gun recoils backward.
  • Total momentum is conserved.
  • The gun's recoil velocity is much smaller because its mass is much greater than the bullet's mass.
  • Gun recoil also illustrates Newton's Third Law.
66. Seat Belt
  • Seat belts restrain passengers during sudden deceleration.
  • Without a seat belt, inertia tends to keep the passenger moving forward.
  • Seat belts increase stopping time and spread force over stronger parts of the body.
  • They reduce the risk of collision with the vehicle interior.
67. Airbag
  • An airbag increases the time over which a passenger's momentum changes.
  • Increasing impact time reduces average force.
  • Airbags also distribute force over a larger body area.
  • Airbags supplement seat belts rather than replace them.
68. Force and Pressure
  • Pressure is force per unit area.
  • P = F/A.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • The same force produces greater pressure over a smaller area.
  • Sharp tools concentrate force over a small area.
  • Wide tyres reduce pressure by distributing force over a larger area.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pressure → Force/Area

69. Torque
  • Torque is the turning effect of a force.
  • Torque depends on force and perpendicular distance from the axis.
  • τ = rF sinθ.
  • SI unit is newton metre.
  • A long spanner requires less force to produce the same torque.
  • Door handles are positioned far from hinges to increase turning effect.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Torque → Turning Effect

70. Couple
  • A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces separated by a distance.
  • The resultant force of a couple is zero.
  • The couple produces rotation.
  • Moment of a couple equals one force multiplied by perpendicular separation.
  • Turning a steering wheel can involve a couple.
71. Force and Work
  • Mechanical work is done when a force causes displacement.
  • W = Fs cosθ.
  • If there is no displacement, mechanical work is zero.
  • If force is perpendicular to displacement, work done by that force is zero.
  • Force and work are different physical quantities.
  • Force is vector; work is scalar.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Holding a heavy object stationary → Muscles expend biological energy, but mechanical work on the stationary object is zero.

72. Force and Acceleration
  • Acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force for fixed mass.
  • a = F/m.
  • Doubling net force doubles acceleration if mass remains constant.
  • Doubling mass halves acceleration for the same net force.
  • Force changes velocity, not necessarily speed alone.
73. Force and Deformation
  • Forces can stretch materials.
  • Forces can compress materials.
  • Forces can bend materials.
  • Forces can twist materials.
  • Elastic deformation disappears after removal of force within the elastic range.
  • Plastic deformation remains after the force is removed.
74. Elastic Force
  • Elastic force tends to restore a deformed object toward its original configuration.
  • Springs exert elastic restoring forces.
  • Elastic force is approximately proportional to deformation within the Hookean range.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, permanent deformation can occur.
75. Tension vs Compression
  • Tension tends to stretch a material.
  • Compression tends to shorten or squeeze a material.
  • Cables are designed mainly to withstand tension.
  • Columns are commonly designed to withstand compression.
  • Beams can experience both tension and compression during bending.
76. Shear Force
  • Shear force acts parallel to a surface or cross-section.
  • It tends to make adjacent layers slide relative to each other.
  • Scissors produce shear forces when cutting.
  • Bolts and rivets may be subjected to shear loads.
77. Force Fields
  • A field describes the influence of a force-producing source throughout space.
  • Gravitational fields act on masses.
  • Electric fields act on electric charges.
  • Magnetic fields act on moving charges and magnetic dipoles.
  • Field strength can vary with position.
78. Gravitational Field
  • Gravitational field strength at a point is force per unit mass.
  • g = F/m.
  • SI unit is N/kg.
  • N/kg is dimensionally equivalent to m/s².
  • Gravitational field direction is the direction of force on a test mass.
  • Near Earth, the field is directed approximately toward Earth's centre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gravitational Field Strength → N/kg

79. Electric Field
  • Electric field strength is force per unit positive test charge.
  • E = F/q.
  • SI unit is N/C.
  • Electric field points in the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
  • Electric field lines emerge from positive charges and terminate on negative charges in electrostatic diagrams.
80. Magnetic Field
  • A magnetic field is produced by magnets and moving electric charges.
  • Magnetic field is represented by B.
  • SI unit of magnetic flux density is tesla.
  • Field lines outside a bar magnet are conventionally drawn from north pole to south pole.
  • Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops.
81. Force Meter
  • A force meter measures force.
  • A spring balance is a common force-measuring instrument.
  • Spring balances operate using elastic deformation.
  • Force is commonly measured in newtons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Force → Spring Balance → Newton

82. Spring Balance vs Beam Balance
  • Spring balance measures force or weight.
  • Beam balance compares masses.
  • Spring-balance reading changes if gravitational acceleration changes.
  • Beam balance comparison of masses is largely independent of local g because both sides are affected similarly.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Spring balance → Weight.

Beam balance → Mass.

83. Newton — Important Facts
  • Isaac Newton formulated the three laws of motion.
  • Newton formulated the universal law of gravitation.
  • Newton's major work Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published in 1687.
  • It is commonly called the Principia.
  • Newton's work established much of classical mechanics.
  • The SI unit of force is named after Newton.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton → Laws of Motion + Gravitation → Principia 1687

84. Galileo and Force
  • Galileo Galilei studied motion and falling bodies.
  • Galileo helped establish that continuous force is not required to maintain uniform motion in the absence of resistance.
  • His work contributed to the later development of the concept of inertia.
  • Galileo's studies prepared the foundation for Newtonian mechanics.
85. Aristotle — Historical Contrast
  • Aristotle believed that continued motion required continued force in many terrestrial situations.
  • Friction made this interpretation appear reasonable in everyday experience.
  • Galileo's studies helped separate the effects of friction from ideal motion.
  • Newton's First Law later formalised inertia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aristotle → Older motion view

Galileo/Newton → Inertia-based mechanics

86. Force in Uniform Motion
  • An object moving at constant velocity has zero acceleration.
  • Therefore its net force is zero.
  • Force is not required to maintain constant velocity in an ideal frictionless environment.
  • Force is required to change velocity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Force causes acceleration, not velocity itself.

87. Force in Circular Motion
  • A body moving at constant speed in a circle has changing velocity because direction changes.
  • Therefore it has acceleration.
  • The acceleration is directed toward the centre.
  • A net inward force is therefore necessary.
  • If the inward force disappears, the body moves approximately along a tangent.
88. Free-Body Diagram
  • A free-body diagram shows forces acting on a selected object.
  • The object is isolated conceptually from its surroundings.
  • Each force is represented by an arrow.
  • Arrow direction shows force direction.
  • Arrow length may represent force magnitude.
  • Free-body diagrams help determine resultant force.
📌 Remember

Free-body diagram → Only forces acting on the chosen body

89. Common Forces in Free-Body Diagrams
  • Weight → Downward toward Earth.
  • Normal reaction → Perpendicular to surface.
  • Friction → Opposes relative motion or tendency to slide.
  • Tension → Along rope or string.
  • Applied force → Direction of push or pull.
  • Drag → Opposite motion through fluid.
  • Buoyant force → Upward in fluid.
90. Force on an Inclined Plane
  • Weight acts vertically downward.
  • Weight can be resolved into components relative to the plane.
  • Component parallel to plane = mg sinθ.
  • Component perpendicular to plane = mg cosθ.
  • For a simple object with no other perpendicular forces, normal reaction = mg cosθ.
  • Friction acts along the surface opposing motion or tendency to move.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Incline:

Parallel → mg sinθ

Perpendicular → mg cosθ

91. Equilibrium of Forces
  • Translational equilibrium requires vector sum of forces to be zero.
  • ΣF = 0.
  • Rotational equilibrium requires sum of torques to be zero.
  • An object can be stationary or move with constant velocity under translational equilibrium.
  • Static equilibrium requires both force and torque balance.
92. Principle of Moments
  • For a body in rotational equilibrium, clockwise moment equals anticlockwise moment.
  • Moment = Force × Perpendicular distance.
  • The principle is used in balances and levers.
  • A small force can balance a larger force if applied farther from the pivot.
93. Force in a Lever
  • A lever rotates about a fulcrum.
  • Effort is the applied force.
  • Load is the resistance.
  • For equilibrium, effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
  • A longer effort arm reduces the required effort.
94. Mechanical Advantage
  • Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort.
  • MA = Load/Effort.
  • Mechanical advantage greater than one indicates force multiplication.
  • Mechanical advantage has no unit.
  • Machines do not create energy even when they multiply force.
95. Force and Safety
  • Crumple zones increase collision time and absorb kinetic energy.
  • Airbags increase collision time and area of force distribution.
  • Seat belts prevent occupants from continuing forward because of inertia.
  • Helmets deform to absorb energy and reduce peak force.
  • Soft landing surfaces increase stopping time.
96. Force and Sports
  • A batsman changes the momentum of a ball by applying force.
  • Follow-through increases the time over which force is applied.
  • A cricketer catching a ball moves the hands backward to reduce force.
  • Sprinters push the ground backward and receive forward reaction force.
  • Spikes improve friction between athlete and track.
97. Force and Vehicles
  • Engine or motor provides driving force.
  • Friction between tyres and road enables acceleration and turning.
  • Brakes use friction to reduce speed.
  • Air resistance opposes motion.
  • At constant speed on a level road, driving force balances resistive forces.
  • During acceleration, driving force exceeds resistive forces.
98. Important Force Formulae
  • Newton's Second Law → F = ma.
  • Momentum → p = mv.
  • Impulse → J = FΔt = Δp.
  • Weight → W = mg.
  • Gravitation → F = Gm₁m₂/r².
  • Centripetal force → F = mv²/r.
  • Pressure → P = F/A.
  • Spring force → F = −kx.
  • Friction limit → F = μN in the simple model.
  • Torque → τ = rF sinθ.
  • Electric force → F = kq₁q₂/r² in magnitude.
  • Gravitational field → g = F/m.
  • Electric field → E = F/q.
99. Important SI Units
  • Force → newton.
  • Mass → kilogram.
  • Acceleration → m/s².
  • Momentum → kg m/s.
  • Impulse → N s.
  • Weight → newton.
  • Gravitational constant → N m² kg⁻².
  • Gravitational field strength → N/kg.
  • Electric field strength → N/C.
  • Magnetic flux density → tesla.
  • Pressure → pascal.
  • Torque → N m.
  • Coefficient of friction → No unit.
100. Must-Memorise Force Pairs
  • Force → Newton.
  • Mass → Inertia.
  • Newton I → Inertia.
  • Newton II → F = ma.
  • Newton III → Action-Reaction.
  • Momentum → mv.
  • Impulse → Δp.
  • Gravity → Mass attraction.
  • Electrostatic → Charges.
  • Strong force → Nucleus / quarks.
  • Weak force → Beta decay.
  • Friction → Opposes relative motion.
  • Normal → Perpendicular to surface.
  • Tension → Along string.
  • Drag → Fluid resistance.
  • Buoyancy → Upward fluid force.
  • Centripetal → Inward.
  • Torque → Turning effect.
  • Spring → Hooke's Law.
101. TNPSC Traps
  • Force is a vector quantity.
  • Work and energy are scalars.
  • Newton is the SI unit of force.
  • Net force zero means zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity.
  • Balanced forces can act on a moving object.
  • A body can move at constant velocity without a net force.
  • Inertia is not a force.
  • Mass measures inertia.
  • Newton's Second Law is fundamentally related to rate of change of momentum.
  • Action and reaction act on different bodies.
  • Momentum is conserved in an isolated system.
  • Impulse equals change in momentum.
  • Longer stopping time reduces average impact force for the same momentum change.
  • Normal reaction is not always equal to weight.
  • Friction can be useful.
  • Rolling friction is generally less than sliding friction.
  • Coefficient of friction has no unit.
  • Gravity is always attractive between ordinary masses.
  • Electrostatic force may attract or repel.
  • Strong nuclear interaction is strongest among the four fundamental interactions.
  • Gravity is weakest at the particle scale.
  • Weak force is involved in beta decay.
  • Rocket propulsion does not require air.
  • Centripetal force acts inward.
  • Centrifugal force is a pseudo force in rotating frames.
  • Constant-speed circular motion has acceleration.
  • Spring balance measures weight/force.
  • Beam balance compares mass.
  • G and g are different quantities.
  • Mass remains unchanged on the Moon; weight becomes about one-sixth.
  • At terminal velocity, acceleration is zero.
  • Magnetic force on a moving charge can alter direction without changing speed when force remains perpendicular to motion.
102. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Force → Push/Pull.
  • Unit → Newton.
  • Vector → Magnitude + direction.
  • Balanced → Net force zero.
  • Unbalanced → Acceleration.
  • Newton I → Inertia.
  • Newton II → F = ma.
  • Newton III → Action-Reaction.
  • Momentum → mv.
  • Impulse → Δp.
  • Normal → Perpendicular.
  • Tension → Along rope.
  • Friction → Opposes sliding.
  • Drag → Fluid resistance.
  • Gravity → Attractive.
  • Coulomb → Charge force.
  • Strong → Strongest.
  • Weak → Beta decay.
  • Weight → mg.
  • G → Universal constant.
  • g → Local gravity.
  • Moon weight → 1/6.
  • Centripetal → Inward.
  • Centrifugal → Apparent outward.
  • Spring → −kx.
  • Torque → Turning effect.
  • Pressure → F/A.
  • Rocket → Third Law + Momentum.
  • Left-hand rule → Motor force.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Force means? → Push or pull.
  • SI unit of force? → Newton.
  • Force is scalar or vector? → Vector.
  • 1 newton equals? → 1 kg m/s².
  • Zero resultant force means? → Zero acceleration.
  • Can a body move when net force is zero? → Yes, with constant velocity.
  • Forces with zero resultant? → Balanced forces.
  • Forces producing acceleration? → Unbalanced forces.
  • Examples of contact forces? → Friction, tension, normal reaction and drag.
  • Examples of non-contact forces? → Gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces.
  • Four fundamental interactions? → Strong, electromagnetic, weak and gravitational.
  • Strongest fundamental interaction? → Strong interaction.
  • Weakest at particle scale? → Gravity.
  • Force involved in beta decay? → Weak nuclear force.
  • Force binding the atomic nucleus? → Residual strong nuclear force.
  • Newton's First Law? → Law of Inertia.
  • Measure of inertia? → Mass.
  • Is inertia a force? → No.
  • Inertia of rest example? → Passenger falling backward when bus starts suddenly.
  • Inertia of motion example? → Passenger falling forward when bus stops suddenly.
  • Newton's Second Law for constant mass? → F = ma.
  • Acceleration for fixed mass is proportional to? → Net force.
  • Acceleration for fixed force is inversely proportional to? → Mass.
  • Newton's Third Law? → Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
  • Action-reaction forces act on? → Different bodies.
  • Momentum formula? → p = mv.
  • Momentum is scalar or vector? → Vector.
  • SI unit of momentum? → kg m/s.
  • When is momentum conserved? → In an isolated system with no net external force.
  • Impulse formula? → FΔt.
  • Impulse equals? → Change in momentum.
  • SI unit of impulse? → N s.
  • Why does a cricketer move hands backward while catching? → To increase stopping time and reduce force.
  • Force perpendicular to a surface? → Normal reaction.
  • Force transmitted through rope? → Tension.
  • Force opposing relative motion? → Friction.
  • Friction before sliding? → Static friction.
  • Maximum static friction? → Limiting friction.
  • Friction during sliding? → Kinetic friction.
  • Which is generally less: rolling or sliding friction? → Rolling friction.
  • Coefficient of friction has unit? → No.
  • Why are ball bearings used? → To reduce sliding friction by rolling.
  • Resistance offered by fluid? → Drag.
  • At terminal velocity, net force? → Zero.
  • At terminal velocity, acceleration? → Zero.
  • Universal gravitation formulated by? → Isaac Newton.
  • Gravitational law formula? → F = Gm₁m₂/r².
  • Value of G approximately? → 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
  • Acceleration due to gravity near Earth? → About 9.8 m/s².
  • SI unit of g? → m/s².
  • G and g same? → No.
  • Weight formula? → W = mg.
  • Mass SI unit? → kg.
  • Weight SI unit? → N.
  • Weight on Moon relative to Earth? → About one-sixth.
  • Mass on Moon compared with Earth? → Same.
  • In vacuum, which falls faster: heavy or light object? → Both have the same gravitational acceleration.
  • Net inward force for circular motion? → Centripetal force.
  • Centripetal-force formula? → mv²/r.
  • Direction of centripetal force? → Toward centre.
  • Apparent outward force in rotating frame? → Centrifugal force.
  • Why are roads banked? → To assist centripetal force and reduce dependence on friction.
  • Electrostatic force law? → Coulomb's Law.
  • Like electric charges? → Repel.
  • Unlike electric charges? → Attract.
  • Can gravitational force repel ordinary masses? → No.
  • Magnetic force on current-carrying conductor gives principle of? → Electric motor.
  • Rule for direction of motor force? → Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.
  • Left-hand thumb represents? → Force or motion.
  • Rocket works mainly on? → Newton's Third Law and conservation of momentum.
  • Can rocket work in vacuum? → Yes.
  • Recoil of gun demonstrates? → Newton's Third Law and conservation of momentum.
  • Buoyant force direction? → Upward.
  • Buoyant force equals according to Archimedes? → Weight of displaced fluid.
  • Pressure formula? → F/A.
  • Torque means? → Turning effect of force.
  • Torque formula? → rF sinθ.
  • Spring restoring force law? → Hooke's Law.
  • Spring-force formula? → F = −kx.
  • Instrument measuring force? → Spring balance.
  • Spring balance measures? → Force/weight.
  • Beam balance measures? → Mass by comparison.
  • Net force during constant-speed straight-line motion? → Zero.
  • Does constant-speed circular motion have net force? → Yes, inward centripetal force.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Newton I → Inertia; Newton II → F = ma; Newton III → Action–Reaction; Momentum → mv; Impulse → Δp; Gravity → Gm₁m₂/r².
